findings.claim: The unit is named 'chemistry-paper-1' and a sibling unit is named 'chemistry-paper-2', which implies a two-paper chemistry split.
findings.truth: J260 has ONE chemistry paper: Foundation J260/02 and Higher J260/06, each 95 marks, 1 hour 45 minutes, 26.4% of the GCSE, assessing C1-C6 plus BCP7 and BCP8. Papers 1-4 are Biology /01, Chemistry /02, Physics /03 and Combined /04 (75 marks, 1 hour 45 minutes, 20.8%); Papers 5-8 mirror them at Higher. No lesson in this unit states a paper structure, so there is nothing wrong in the text and nothing should be renamed. Lesson-to-chapter mapping recorded here: L1 = C1.1 (outcomes 5-6), L2 = C1.2, L3 = C1.3, L4 = C1.4, L5 = C2.1, L6 = C2.2, L7 = C2.3 plus C3.1 and C4.2, L8 = C2.4 plus C5.2 (outcomes 1-3). Sibling unit science-ocr-b/chemistry-paper-2 exists in the queue (8 lessons, queued) and covers C3.1-C3.4, C4.1-C4.4 and C5.1.
findings.evidence: spec assessment overview (Content Overview / Assessment Overview tables, both tiers); chapter headings C1-C6

findings.claim: Some assessable outcomes of C1 and C2 are taught in neither chemistry unit.
findings.truth: Not taught anywhere in chemistry-paper-1 or chemistry-paper-2: C1.1.1-C1.1.4 (particle model, states of matter, energy transfers and forces at change of state, predicting state from data; C1.1.2 is bold, so Higher only), and C1.1.7-C1.1.8 (carbon monoxide and particulates from incomplete combustion, sulfur dioxide from sulfur impurities, oxides of nitrogen, and the abatement measures: catalytic converters, low sulfur petrol, gas scrubbers). Also absent: C1.4.2, the test for chlorine with blue litmus paper (PAGC1). The particle model is covered on the physics side (physics-paper-2 L7), but it is assessable on the chemistry paper too. Options: add one air-quality lesson to this unit (it is the natural home, C1.1), or extend L4 with the chlorine test. Recommendation: build one new lesson on combustion pollutants and air quality, and fold the chlorine test into L4.
findings.evidence: spec C1.1 outcomes 1-4, 7-8; C1.4.2 PAGC1; corpus lesson titles for both science-ocr-b chemistry units

findings.claim: Ice cores are taught as a line of evidence for Earth's EARLY atmosphere, in the content, the conclusion, the exam tip, a 4-mark answer key, a match knowledge check stem and a flashcard.
findings.truth: Ice cores reach back only about 800,000 years. Earth's early atmosphere is 4.6 to 2.7 billion years old, so ice cores cannot sample it; they are evidence for recent atmospheric change (C1.3). The spec names the types and chemical composition of ancient rocks, and fossil evidence of early life, as the evidence base for C1.1. The lesson's own 6-mark key already concedes the limitation, which is why that key is left alone.
findings.evidence: spec C1.1 narrative and outcome 5; settled fact (EPICA Dome C ice core about 800,000 years)

findings.claim: The temperature-change formula reads 'ΔT = Tₙₐˣ − TₓₜₐⱿₜ'.
findings.truth: The subscripts are corrupted characters, not 'max' and 'start'. Replaced with 'ΔT = T<sub>max</sub> − T<sub>start</sub>'. Narration would also have read the garbage aloud.
findings.evidence: recomputation not needed; character corruption is self-evident

findings.claim: 'Breaking bond energy requires energy — breaking bonds is endothermic'.
findings.truth: You break bonds, not bond energy. The sentence was rewritten so the definition of bond energy is a separate clause and the physics is stated once.
findings.evidence: spec C1.2 narrative: 'Breaking bonds requires energy (the activation energy) whilst making bonds gives out energy'

findings.claim: A higher-only wrapper hid the whole 'Bond Energies' section, including 'breaking bonds requires energy, making bonds releases energy'.
findings.truth: That statement is plain (not bold) in the C1.2 narrative, so it is assessed at both tiers and a Foundation student must see it. Only outcome C1.2.5, 'calculate energy changes in a chemical reaction by considering bond breaking and bond making energies', is bold and therefore Higher only. The wrapper has been narrowed to enclose the calculation collapsible alone, and that collapsible now carries a '(Higher tier)' label. Div open and close counts are unchanged.
findings.evidence: spec bold file C1.2: narrative and outcome 5 bold; outcomes 1-4 and 6 plain

findings.claim: Match knowledge check offered right-hand options 'Exothermic', 'Endothermic' and 'Endothermic (requires energy input)'.
findings.truth: Two options are synonymous, so 'Products at higher energy than reactants' matches either one and the item cannot be marked fairly. The third row now pairs 'Lowers the activation energy without changing product energy' with 'Catalyst', both taught in this lesson, and the stem was widened to suit.
findings.evidence: internal consistency; lesson n15 and key fact n16 teach the catalyst point

findings.claim: A bond-energy calculation practice question and two flashcards test Higher-tier-only content with no tier flag.
findings.truth: C1.2.5 is bold in the spec, so the calculation is Higher tier only. The practice question is now prefixed '(Higher tier)'; the two flashcards carry the tag at the end of the question, per house convention.

findings.claim: The lesson teaches calorimetry with Q = mcΔT (c = 4.18 J/g/°C) as a worked example and sets a 4-mark practice question on it.
findings.truth: J260 places specific heat capacity and 'change in internal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × change in temperature' in the physics chapter P6, in J/kg/°C. C1.2 has no calorimetry outcome; its practical is qualitative ('Investigate different chemical reactions to find out if they are exothermic or endothermic') and outcome 1 asks only for the direction of the temperature change. Both worked examples are arithmetically correct (50 × 4.18 × 19 = 3971 J; 50 × 4.18 × 21 = 4389 J), so nothing here is wrong, only out of scope for the chemistry paper. Options: (a) keep it as enrichment and add one line saying the calculation itself is assessed in physics; (b) cut the worked-example collapsible and practice question 5 and replace them with the qualitative method. Recommendation: (a) - option (b) rips out a narration block and a question with no gain. Not edited.
findings.evidence: spec C1.2 outcomes 1-6; spec P6 specific heat capacity outcomes

findings.claim: Mark scheme contained raw LaTeX: '\(\Delta T = 41 - 20 = 21\)°C' and '\(Q = 50 \times 4.18 \times 21 = 4389\)'.
findings.truth: Practice question text is written with textContent and the mark scheme is not passed to KaTeX (js/main.js renders KaTeX only into study-notes, conclusion and exam-tip), so the delimiters show as literal backslashes. Rewritten in unicode.
findings.evidence: js/main.js showQuestion() and lesson-loader.js KaTeX targets

findings.claim: Mark scheme opens 'Award 1 mark for any of: ...'.
findings.truth: 'Award N marks for' is a banned board rubric phrase; the house validator rejects the entire unit on it. Rewritten as house wording with a [1 mark] tag.

findings.claim: Two mark schemes contained raw LaTeX '\(CO_2\)'.
findings.truth: Replaced with the unicode CO₂, as elsewhere in the unit.
findings.evidence: js/main.js practice rendering (textContent, no KaTeX pass)

findings.claim: The 6-mark scenario reads 'a small island community with a stream but no access to the sea'.
findings.truth: An island cannot have no access to the sea. The mark scheme only needs fresh water to be available so that desalination is unnecessary, so the clause was replaced with 'that has a freshwater stream'.
findings.evidence: internal consistency with the question's own key

findings.claim: Live lesson text reads '... be less reactive than chlorine (which has configuration 2, 8, 7 at period 3 — wait, that IS chlorine: 17 electrons)'.
findings.truth: A drafting aside was left in the published content and the surrounding reasoning contradicts itself. Rewritten: 2, 8, 7 is chlorine (17 electrons); bromine (2, 8, 18, 7) is one period lower and less reactive.

findings.claim: The key for 'element X has electronic configuration 2, 8, 1' says 'compares with potassium to suggest reactivity is between sodium and potassium'.
findings.truth: 2, 8, 1 is 11 electrons, which is sodium itself. The key now says X is sodium, so it is more reactive than lithium and less reactive than potassium.

findings.claim: Mark scheme contained raw LaTeX '\(Br_2 + 2KI \rightarrow 2KBr + I_2\)'.
findings.truth: Replaced with unicode 'Br₂ + 2KI → 2KBr + I₂'. The equation itself is balanced and correct.

findings.claim: Mark scheme reads 'magnesium loses two electrons to form α₂⁺'.
findings.truth: The magnesium ion is Mg²⁺. The published key gave a corrupted Greek alpha with a subscript 2, which a student copying the key would reproduce.

findings.claim: Practice question 3 asks the student to balance '\(Fe + O_2 \rightarrow Fe_2O_3\)', and three mark schemes carry the same raw LaTeX.
findings.truth: The question text is set with textContent and never passed to KaTeX, so the student sees the backslashes instead of the equation they must balance. All rewritten in unicode. The chemistry was checked and is right: 4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃ balances, and the CaCO₃ figures are exact (M_r 100 → CaO 56 + CO₂ 44).
findings.evidence: js/main.js showQuestion(); recomputation of relative formula masses from the spec periodic table

summary: Eight lessons checked against OCR Twenty First Century Science B J260 (Combined). Seventeen lesson-level findings: three HIGH (a banned 'Award 1 mark for' rubric that fails the house validator, a drafting aside left live in L6, and a corrupted Mg2+ in an L7 mark scheme), plus a wrong tier wrapper in L2, ice cores taught as evidence for the early atmosphere in L1, and raw LaTeX in plain-text practice fields across four lessons. Every worked calculation recomputed and all were correct. Three unit-level ADJUDICATE items: the paper mapping (J260 has one chemistry paper), C1 outcomes taught nowhere, and Q = mcDeltaT being a physics-chapter equation.
